prompt: I'm a working programmer and I'm tired of grand architecture talk and hype around every new platform. Write an essay on why smart people drift into over-abstraction and why it's mostly noise.
Hegel dominated philosophy for a century and is now mostly a punchline. Write a blog post about what to make of a thinker whose reputation swung that far, and what it might mean for our own thinking.

I'm about to turn thirty and keep wondering what actually changes between being a teenager and being an adult, beyond the obvious. Write a reflective essay on what we lose and gain as we grow out of youth, maybe drawing on a poet or two.
It's my birthday and I'm wondering whether getting older really makes you wiser, or whether the things I think I've learned are something else. Write a candid, self-skeptical essay on that.
Write an essay about the danger of drawing firm rules of thumb from one or two memorable cases, with a few examples from tech forecasting, politics and anything else that fits.

Why do some public predictors get endlessly mocked as wrong while others get endlessly credited as prophets, whatever actually happens? I'm thinking about starting to make public predictions and want to know how to avoid getting burned. Write it up as a blog post.

Why are flu and colds so much worse in winter? Everyone gives a quick answer (cold air, dry air, being stuck indoors, vitamin D) but I suspect the real story is messier. Write an exploratory essay that tests the popular explanations against what we actually see, and says what it might mean for COVID.

San Francisco seems visibly less chaotic than it did a year or two ago, even though nobody built the jails or mental hospitals people said were needed. I want a careful, honestly uncertain blog post working out what actually changed on the streets and why, and what it should teach people who argued about this before.

Rationalists love to say you should correct for your biases, and yet 'you're only saying that because you're biased' tends to wreck conversations. Write an essay on why bias arguments so often go nowhere, and whether there's any good way to use them.

Review Bruce Fink's A Clinical Introduction to Lacanian Psychoanalysis for a skeptical reader who likes AI alignment and psychiatry. Be upfront that Lacan is famously obscure and you may not have understood it, and tell me how desire and the diagnoses work in the book as best you can.
Everyone says life is short. Is it actually, or is that just a complaint about it being finite? And if it is short, what should that change about how we live? Write an essay on this.

Most people can't remember much of what they supposedly learned in school. I'm curious what that implies about whether school does any good. Write an essay working through it from first principles, using whatever evidence on memory and knowledge you think is relevant.
Write a blog post on a recent study that tested how well doctors understand statistics (p-values, mammogram probabilities). I want a funny but fair look at what it shows and what it doesn't.

Investors keep talking about using data to predict which startups will succeed. Write an essay about the pitfalls of predicting the future from historical data when the thing you're measuring keeps changing underneath you.

I've read plenty of self-help success books and never trust them. Someone told me to look at Trump's 1988 book The Art of the Deal, as a how-to on persuasion and success. Write a book review: is there anything to learn from it, and what does it reveal about the man who wrote it?
Does it matter whether coworkers eat lunch together? Write a short essay about lunch at work, from the point of view of someone running a company who has strong feelings about it.

A new randomized trial found Freudian-style therapy did about as well as cognitive behavioral therapy for depression. I'm a psychiatry resident and I was taught that psychoanalysis was debunked. Write a blog post on what to make of this and how we ended up believing what we believed.

Your company has only ever sold tools to software developers, and you've just launched a simple team-coordination app meant for everyone. Write a blog post about what it means to build a 'horizontal' product versus a 'vertical' one, and what you learned about why the great general-purpose apps succeed.

Write a short, funny-but-serious essay about how a whole body of good work (a person, a field, a movement) gets reduced in public memory to its single worst moment. Is that unfair, and do you honestly avoid doing it yourself?

Do public awareness campaigns actually change behavior? Everyone seems to have a pet example of one that worked and one that flopped. Write an essay that tries to make sense of the pattern, and be honest about how much you can really conclude.

I tried eating mindfully once and noticed the food stopped tasting good after a few bites, and then I felt worse than before I started. Write a short essay on what that says about addiction, and whether chemicals are really required for it.

I keep hearing that you are the average of the five people you spend the most time with. It feels too crude. Write an essay on how the people and books around us shape who we are, and what it means to take care of that surrounding context, including what authenticity could mean.

Why do movie tickets cost the same whether the film is a hit or a flop, when basic economics says prices should vary with demand? Write a short, opinionated piece, and bring in what it might mean for how digital music gets priced.

There's another round of hand-wringing about how few women there are in Silicon Valley startups. You're a bootstrapped software founder living in Japan whose customers are mostly women. Write a frank, contrarian blog post about the debate and what the Valley might be getting wrong.

Write a deadpan satirical piece in the style of the hot takes that blame everything on late capitalism and 'modern pathologies', except applied to things that are very obviously ancient. Pick a handful of absurd targets and make the fake-critical argument with a straight face.

I just read about the strangest novel of the 18th century, apparently a book narrated by something absurd and full of coded political satire. Write me a book-review-style essay on it: how the novel as a form got to the point where such a book was possible, what drove its author to write it, and whether it's any good.
Write an essay about moral debts that have no natural limit, like what we owe our parents or our society. Where do such obligations come from, and how should anyone live with them?
Write a casual blog post about what a team member (not the manager) can do to make their team a great one to work on. Base it on a conversation with a friend who's good at this.

It's late 2009 and developers are increasingly furious about the iPhone App Store's approval process. Write an essay on why this matters more to Apple than Apple seems to think, and what it might lead to.

Everyone online suddenly says there's an underpopulation crisis. Write a blog post that takes the worry seriously but is skeptical of it, going through the different versions of the concern (extinction, shrinking countries, aging, fewer innovators, dysgenics) and how much each one should actually bother us.

People keep telling me you can't assign probabilities to things when you have no model, like first contact with aliens or a risky long-shot bet. I think that's wrong. Write a piece arguing about whether we can and should use probability without a model.
Write an essay about what happens to your ideas when you try to put them into words. Is it possible to have fully formed ideas about something you've never written about?

Software startups are often founded by people fresh out of school, but young teams building CPUs almost always seem to fail. Write an essay on why experience matters so much more in hardware than software.

Write an essay about the procedures and approval steps that companies pile up as they grow, meant to protect against mistakes. What do they actually cost, and who pays? I'm especially curious how this affects programmers.

California's billionaire wealth tax ballot measure looks badly drafted, and I keep hearing it's being pushed by a healthcare union rather than by generic left-wing activists. Write an essay on who is really behind it and why that changes how we should read the whole thing.

Write an essay arguing that people who work in or near tech should take the development of machines smarter than humans seriously as a risk. I'm especially interested in why smart people tend to wave the danger away, either as impossible or as very far off.

Write a book review of Ernst Jünger's novella On the Marble Cliffs for a general reader who has never heard of it. I'd like it to cover the historical context, what the prose is actually like (and the translation question), what happens, and what you think the book is really for.
Write a stoic-flavored manifesto on bracing for hard times and training your reactions. Short, direct lines.

I'm about to start applying for summer internships. You've read hundreds of applications from a hiring manager's chair. Write me a candid post on what makes a résumé and cover letter get tossed, and what helps.

Everyone says to grow as a programmer you need side projects, conference talks and books in your evenings. I don't want to do extra work after hours. Write a post about how to keep learning and get really good mostly during the workday.
Write a short essay about a piece of music that makes you feel more human: Shostakovich's eighth string quartet. Give me the history behind it and what you hear in it.
I'm working on something early and people keep asking whether it's a 'real company' yet. Write an essay on whether it matters if an early-stage venture is thought of as a project or a company.

I want a book review of Jordan Peterson's Twelve Rules for Life from someone who went in expecting to mock it. Say what actually works about the book, what doesn't, and what kind of thing it really is.
I keep making big life decisions and regretting them. Is there a simple way to think about what I should be choosing? Write it up as a short essay.

Write a personal essay about how audiences shape what a writer (or any creative person) is able to say. Can writing for other people and writing for yourself ever be compatible, or does an audience always distort you?

Heartbleed spread through the whole industry in about a day and got hundreds of thousands of people patching. Write a blog post for open source developers about what that says about marketing, and why the OSS world should take it more seriously than it does.

A psychiatrist treated a patient who took LSD once and has hallucinated ever since. Write an essay on how a drug that leaves the body in hours could cause permanent changes, and what that might say about other lasting side effects.
Compare the Forbes 400 lists from the early 1980s and from 2020. How has the way people get very rich in America changed, and why? Write it up as an essay, written from the vantage point of 2021.

Headlines say drug testing welfare applicants found almost no drug users. Dig into whether those numbers mean what the media says, and what it says about honesty in journalism when you're on the right side of an argument.

A lot of people blame the Supreme Court's Griggs v. Duke Power decision for why employers demand college degrees for jobs that don't need them. Is that a fair diagnosis? Write a short essay testing it.

Friends at a party insisted that the pharaoh Djoser was the real inspiration behind both the god Osiris and the Biblical Joseph. Write up what you'd find if you actually dug into whether either connection holds up.
Write a book review of Kerouac's On the Road. Make it funny and opinionated, quote the book where it helps, and say what you think the novel is really about and whether it holds up today.

A small pharma company's experimental antidepressant failed its main trial, then put out a press release months later saying it worked after all, and the stock jumped. I'm a psychiatrist who badly wanted it to be real. Write a blog post working out whether to believe the new results, and why the market might believe them anyway.

I'm an engineer at a mid-sized tech company and I'd like to make our hiring a bit fairer without starting a huge political fight. Write a short blog post making the case for one small, practical change engineers can push for in how their company runs technical interviews.

Newspapers love to point out that places like Denmark and Finland have high antidepressant use and suicide rates, as if that proves they are secretly dysfunctional. Write an essay on what depression and suicide statistics can and can't tell us about how well a society works.
Write an essay about pseudonyms and online identities, and whether wearing a mask can make you more honest and more capable rather than less.
A founder tells you he's worried he's too soft-hearted to succeed and gives too much away for free. Write a short essay on whether startup founders can afford to be nice.

People say the rich have captured government and bend it to their interests. But doesn't collective action get in the way of that? Write an essay thinking through whether class interests can actually be coordinated.

It's early 2005 and you've noticed that the serious programmers you know are buying Powerbooks. Write a short essay about why hackers are moving to the Mac, what the Mac once meant to people like you, and why a company should care what such a small group of users thinks.

We're reading 'Out of the Tar Pit' in my reading group. The paper leans on Dijkstra's line that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence, and argues informal reasoning matters more than testing. Write a short response essay: do you buy that, especially from the perspective of someone who has built genuinely complex systems?

Write an essay arguing for a political position that mixes free-market tools with real concern for the poor and for minorities. Use concrete policy examples and explain why taxes and subsidies might beat bans and mandates.

Everyone hates Congress and every proposed fix needs Congress to pass it. Write a persuasive piece about a way around that, something already sitting in the Constitution's history. Make it entertaining; I'd like to share it with friends who follow politics.

Satire about TV-addicted, ad-dazed consumers is starting to feel dated, and 'people staring at their phones' already feels like yesterday's critique. Write an essay guessing at what the cultural critics of ten years from now will skewer about how we live online today.

I just finished David Friedman's book on legal systems very different from ours, and I keep wondering what it says about law, the state, and whether the way we do justice is the only workable way. Write a long-form book-review-style essay on it, with your own reactions and reservations.

People in AI safety keep getting accused of wanting to hand the world over to machines. Write an essay defending a more careful position: that humans putting aligned AIs in positions of control might actually serve human interests. Make it concrete by walking through a range of what that could look like, from modest to radical.
Write a cranky blog post about big software companies that keep building grand 'platform' products nobody asked for, and what that does to the rest of the industry.

More and more people I know say they won't have kids because of climate change, AI risk, or because the money would do more good elsewhere. I'm about to start a family myself, and I don't find the usual 'it's natural, just have kids' response convincing as an answer to that. Write a personal essay that takes these social-movement arguments against having children seriously and tries to work out what's really underneath them.
